newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia, under U.S. pressure, targets illicit assets.
newsitem.headline: Colombia, under U.S. pressure, targets illicit assets.

text.p: Colombia said on Friday that it had sent an important message to the United States and international community by passing a tough new anti-drug law aimed at bankrupting its billionaire cocaine merchants.

"This is very important news for the United States," said Foreign Minister Maria Emma Mejia, referring to the so-called asset forfeiture law approved by an overwelming majority in the Senate and House of Representatives late on Thursday.
"I am certain that both the State Department and the White House will see this as a clear sign from Colombia and I'm certain that it will have repercussions there," Mejia said.
"It (the United States) is a country that will seriously understand now that Colombia is committed to cooperating and collaborating in efforts to eradicate drug trafficking," she added.

"We're in the legislative vanguard now," added Justice Minister Carlos Medellin, one of several government ministers who lobbied intensely in Congress for the law's passage. "We can now show the world that we have one of the strongest anti-drug laws there is."

Colombia was rendered a virtual pariah state last March when the United States struck it from a list of countries deemed fully cooperative in the fight against drugs. U.S. officials have warned repeatedly that a second "decertification," when Washington announces its international drug report card on Morch 1, could automatically trigger punitive trade sanctions against the country which is the world's leading cocaine producer and a major supplier of heroin to the United States.

Political analysts say President Ernesto Samper, who has been unable to shake off his drug-tainted image in Washington, clearly had those sanctions in mind when he launched a full court press in Colombia's reluctant Congress for passage of the asset forfeiture law.

It remains to be seen whether the law, which allows for the retroactive seizure of property and assets accumulated by drug lords over the past 20 years, will be enough for Colombia to avert trade sanctions.

But other measures -- including a bill that would increase prison sentences for traffickers -- are pending in Congress. And Samper, who came close to resigning in disgrace 10 months ago because of charges he used drug money for his election campaign, says he has done more than any of his predecessors to crack down on Colombia's drug cartels.

It was, after all, on Samper's watch that the leaders of the powerful Cali cartel were jailed last year. And the asset forfeiture law he championed could lead to the confiscation of hundreds of millions of dollars in illicit real estate holdings and other property.
Even Samper's right-hand man, Interior Minister Horacio Serpa, conceded in a speech to Congress last week that 99 percent of all crimes in Colombia go unpunished, however.

And government critics like Enrique Parejo, a former justice minister and anti-drug crusader, say laws in Colombia often seem to be made only to be broken later on. "We've specialized in that here," Parejo told Reuters in an interview on Friday. "In ways of seeing to it that the laws are never carried out."

Medellin, in a thinly-veiled reference to possible U.S. sanctions, said the law passed on Thursday night would help clean up Colombia's tattered image abroad. But he added that "we're going to continue having problems as long as large quantities of Colombian cocaine and (opium) poppy continue entering the United States and other countries."
